Conies
kō'nēz
n. pl. (rock badgers of the cliffs; a feeble folk that build in the rocks, and one of the four little wise things)
Middle English coni, from Latin cuniculus, a rabbit — the older English name for the rabbit. The Hebrew shaphan is the rock hyrax of the Palestinian cliffs, a small hoofed animal with no defence but its shelter.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Twice the word appears, and both times it is about where the creature lives. The psalmist, cataloguing God's ordering of creation: “The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies” (Psa 104:18) — every creature has been given a place suited to it, which is the psalm's whole argument for providence. And Agur, in his four small wonders: “The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks” (Pro 30:26), one of the “four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise” (Pro 30:24). The animal has no speed, no size, no weapons; its entire wisdom is knowing where to live. Agur does not commend it for overcoming its weakness but for accepting it and building accordingly. The Rock in Scripture is a name of God from Moses' song onward, and a feeble folk that makes its house in the rock is as good a picture of the church as the Old Testament provides.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the coney as a rabbit; and notes the Scripture coney as an animal of the rocks in Palestine, feeble but wise in its habitation.

CONEY, n. A rabbit; a quadruped of the genus Lepus.

The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks. Prov. xxx.

The animal of Scripture so called is supposed to be the hyrax of the rocks of Syria.

CONEY-BURROW, n. A place where rabbits burrow in the earth.

Key Scripture

Psa 104:18 — "The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies."

Pro 30:26 — "The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks;"

Pro 30:24 — "There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise:"

Lev 11:29 — "These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind,"

Modern Corruption

Weakness is treated as a problem to be overcome by effort, while Proverbs 30:26 commends a feeble creature precisely for building where its weakness is answered.

expand to see more

Agur's four small things are wise in different ways — the ants prepare, the locusts keep order, the spider takes hold — and the conies are wise in the least heroic way of all: they know they are feeble and they live in the rocks. There is no suggestion that the creature improves, trains, or compensates. Its wisdom consists entirely in choosing a dwelling that makes its weakness irrelevant. That runs against the whole temper of self-improvement, in its secular form and in its religious one, where a Christian is exhorted to overcome his weakness by discipline and is left ashamed when it persists. Paul was given a thorn that did not leave, and was told, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. His conclusion was not to become strong but to take pleasure in infirmities, that the power of Christ might rest upon him.

The rock is the other half of the lesson and it is not an accident of habitat. He is the Rock, his work is perfect, says the song of Moses; the LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer, says David; and Paul says of the wilderness rock that followed Israel, and that Rock was Christ. A feeble folk making their houses in the rocks is therefore a picture with a name attached. The church is not commended in Scripture for its resources; Paul says not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble are called, and gives the reason — that no flesh should glory in his presence. Psalm 104 completes the thought by insisting the arrangement is God's doing: He appointed the high hills for the wild goats and the rocks for the conies, and He has provided a refuge suited to exactly what His people are.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shaphan (H8227), the coney or rock badger; with sela (H5553), a cliff or rock, and tsur (H6697), the Rock, a name of God.

expand to see more

Hebrew shaphan (H8227) — the coney, the rock hyrax; the rocks for the conies; Psalm 104:18, Proverbs 30:26.

Hebrew sela (H5553) — a cliff, a crag; where they make their houses; Proverbs 30:26.

Hebrew tsur (H6697) — a rock; He is the Rock, his work is perfect; Deuteronomy 32:4.

Hebrew machaseh (H4268) — a refuge; the high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; Psalm 104:18.

Greek astheneia (G769) — weakness, infirmity; my strength is made perfect in weakness; 2 Corinthians 12:9.

Usage

"“The rocks for the conies” — a place appointed to a creature."

"“A feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks” — wisdom that does not deny weakness."

"“Little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise” — Agur's standard for greatness."
